title: Unauthenticated pickle deserialization in the basket cookie enables server-side code execution
description: The basket cookie is entirely attacker-controlled and is passed to pickle.loads without a signature or any other integrity check. A crafted cookie can invoke arbitrary callables during deserialization, before the result is type-checked.
evidence: GET /basket reaches read_basket() and pickle.loads(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(raw)); the cookie is generated by the client and with_basket() provides no MAC or encryption. This is an arbitrary-code-execution path for any request that supplies a basket cookie.

title: Passwordless token refresh accepts unsigned attacker-chosen claims
description: The refresh endpoint decodes the supplied JWT with signature verification disabled and only checks that the referenced user exists. An attacker can create an unsigned token naming another user and receive a freshly signed token for that account.
evidence: POST /auth/refresh with token eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJzdWIiOjF9. returned a valid HS256 token for user id 1. The returned token then authenticates to account/order functionality as that user.

title: Order detail endpoint does not enforce ownership
description: show_order() calls get_order() directly instead of own_order(), so any caller who knows or guesses an order ID can read its status, amounts, items, delivery date, and refunds.
evidence: GET http://127.0.0.1:52091/orders/1 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 and the complete order, including items, paid_pence, and refunds. The require_auth decorator fails open on its abort and this handler never checks g.user.

title: Gift-card balance is disclosed without authentication
description: The balance handler is wrapped in require_auth, but that decorator catches its own 401 exception and still invokes the endpoint. Because balance() does not dereference g.user, the request succeeds for an unauthenticated caller.
evidence: GET http://127.0.0.1:52091/giftcards/HFDEMO10 with no Authorization header returned HTTP 200 with {"balance_pence":1000,"code":"HFDEMO10"}.

title: Product search is SQL-injectable
description: The search term is concatenated directly into a SQL statement. SQL metacharacters can alter the WHERE clause and expose arbitrary rows; further database-specific payloads may alter or extract data.
evidence: GET /products/search?q=%27%20OR%201%3D1%20-- returned all six products, including products that do not match the original search term.

title: Customer display names enable second-order SQL injection in the admin report
description: A customer can set display_name to arbitrary text, and the admin review report later interpolates that stored value into SQL. This lets an ordinary user inject SQL when a staff member views that customer’s report.
evidence: PATCH /account with display_name=' OR 1=1 -- followed by an authenticated GET /admin/reports/reviews?customer_id=1 caused the constructed WHERE clause to become an always-true predicate. The value is written at auth.py:275-277 and later inserted into the f-string at admin.py:141-145.

title: Stored review content is rendered as raw HTML
description: Review bodies are accepted from authenticated users and rendered with the Jinja safe filter. A malicious review therefore executes script in every visitor’s product-page browser context.
evidence: POST /products/1/reviews with body <script>alert(document.domain)</script> returned 201. GET /p/MUG-SPECK then contained the same script tag verbatim at the review-body location.

title: Payment webhook authentication uses a hardcoded, guessable default secret
description: WEBHOOK_SECRET defaults to the source-visible value whsec-local. Deployments that do not override it allow anyone who knows the application defaults to forge payment events.
evidence: The running application accepted an X-Signature HMAC generated with the literal key whsec-local on POST /webhooks/payments and changed a newly created order to processing.

title: Payment webhook trusts an attacker-controlled payment amount
description: After signature verification, the webhook stores event.amount_pence without checking it against the order total or a provider-side payment record. A signed or forged paid event can therefore settle an order for less than its price, including zero.
evidence: A webhook for a £35.00 order with status=paid and amount_pence=0 returned 200; GET /orders/4 then showed status=processing, total_pence=3500, and paid_pence=0.

title: Payment-status timeout fails open as a successful payment
description: A timeout from the payment provider is explicitly converted to status='paid', and the order is moved to processing with paid_pence equal to the order total. A transient provider outage can therefore create unpaid fulfilled orders.
evidence: confirm_payment() catches requests.Timeout at lines 753-756 and immediately takes the paid branch at lines 757-759. No provider confirmation or later rollback is required before fulfillment.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: Password hashes use raw SHA-256 with no salt or work factor. A database compromise permits efficient offline dictionary and brute-force recovery of users’ passwords, including the seeded shared demo password.
evidence: hash_password() is hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest(), and both registration and reset store that value directly in password_hash.

title: Password reset codes use non-cryptographic randomness and have no attempt throttling
description: Reset codes are eight decimal digits generated with random.random(), not a cryptographic generator. reset_confirm has no attempt counter, lockout, or rate limit, so an attacker can make unlimited online guesses during the 30-minute validity window.
evidence: reset_request() creates the code with int(random.random() * 10**8), while reset_confirm() compares a supplied code and changes the password without tracking failed attempts.

title: Request logging records credentials and other sensitive POST data
description: Every POST body is logged, including login passwords, password-reset payloads, bearer-adjacent application data, and potentially payment or personal information. The 2,000-byte truncation does not prevent secret disclosure to log readers or log storage.
evidence: The before_request hook calls request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] for all POST requests. /auth/login and /auth/reset/confirm send passwords in those bodies, so normal authentication traffic is written to application logs.

title: Login reveals whether an email account exists and has no brute-force protection
description: The login response distinguishes an unknown email from a known email with a wrong password, and the endpoint has no rate limiting, lockout, or progressive delay. This supports account enumeration and password guessing.
evidence: POST /auth/login for nobody@mail.test returned {"error":"no account with that email"}, while the same request for admin@hartleyfinch.co.uk with a wrong password returned {"error":"wrong password"}.
